title: Python Environment for Search and Graph Labs
content:
A [virtual environment](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/) keeps this workspace's packages separate from other Python projects. Use Python 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14, which are supported by the current [NetworkX release](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/install.html). PyCharm or VS Code can use the same environment as the terminal.

## Create the environment

Open a terminal in the folder where the search and graph labs will be saved. Check the selected Python version with `python3 --version` on macOS/Linux or `py -3 --version` on Windows. If several versions are installed, select a supported one before creating the environment.

On macOS or Linux:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

In Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
py -3 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

If activation is unavailable, use `.venv/bin/python` on macOS/Linux or `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` on Windows in place of `python` below. Activation changes which interpreter the terminal finds; the environment also works through its explicit interpreter path.

Install the graph, plotting and notebook tools:

```sh
python -m pip install networkx matplotlib jupyterlab
```

If a selected lab supplies `requirements.txt`, use `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` for its declared dependencies. Record the versions that work in this environment with `python -m pip freeze > requirements-local.txt`.

## Run a checkable example

Save the following as `check_environment.py`:

```python
import sys
import networkx as nx
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

graph = nx.path_graph(3)
print(sys.executable)
print(nx.shortest_path(graph, 0, 2))
nx.draw_networkx(graph, pos={node: (node, 0) for node in graph})
plt.axis("off")
plt.savefig("graph-check.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close()
```

Run `python check_environment.py`. The first line should point inside `.venv`; the second should be `[0, 1, 2]`. Open `graph-check.png`: nodes 0, 1 and 2 should form a connected path. The `Agg` plotting backend saves the image without opening a desktop window. The [NetworkX tutorial](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/tutorial.html) explains the graph operations; the [Matplotlib guide](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/quick_start.html) explains figures and plotting.

## Keep the interpreter consistent

Select this same `.venv` interpreter in the editor. For notebook work, run `python -m jupyterlab` from the workspace folder, create a Python notebook, and check `import sys; print(sys.executable)` in its first cell. A different path means the notebook is using a different environment, which can explain imports working in the terminal but failing in the notebook. See [starting JupyterLab](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started/starting.html) for the notebook interface.

Keep an experiment log beside the lab: the command used, the input graph or state, the expected result and the observed result. For this check, record the interpreter path, `[0, 1, 2]` and the generated image.


**Course flow:** Establish one reproducible graph-and-search workspace and a short experiment-log format. Refresh objects only when the state model shows a concrete prerequisite gap.

title: Bridge Positioning between Core Python and ML
content:
## State and decision systems

A search program chooses a sequence of allowed actions. Its inputs are an initial state, transition rules and a goal test. Its output can be a route and an explanation of the choices. A rule system applies conditions written by its author. A learned model instead fits behavior from examples.

For a delivery robot, a state might be its room; a move follows a doorway; the goal is a named destination. Breadth-first search can find a minimum-doorway route when every move has equal cost. If the battery level restricts movement, room alone is insufficient: the state must also record the remaining charge.

The Python prerequisites are functions, lists, dictionaries, sets and simple classes. A list can hold pending states; a dictionary can map a discovered state to its parent. Graph search, rules and game evaluation are the core of this course. Machine Learning develops fitting and evaluating learned models; Data Science in Python develops questions, data preparation and analysis. A search trace supports a claim about the supplied problem and rules, rather than a claim of general intelligence.

title: How to Read an AI Problem Statement
content:
## Specify a problem before searching

Use the directed graph `S: [A, B], A: [G], B: [], G: []`. The initial state is S. Legal actions follow listed arrows; the goal test is equality with G. Each action costs one. A valid solution is S,A,G, with two actions. Reaching B is a dead end, not success.

A state must contain everything needed to determine future legal actions and outcomes. Two visits to the same room with different keys may be different states. An action generator returns only legal successors; a goal test checks the complete requirement. Cost measures the route already taken, whereas a heuristic estimates work still remaining.

An output contract removes ambiguity: a found route includes start and goal; start=goal has a one-state route and zero actions; an unreachable goal has an empty route and no route cost. Invalid input and a valid problem with no solution are different outcomes. Record the neighbor order and tie rule when comparing traces. Several correct algorithms can find different routes with the same cost.

title: Experiment Logging and Reflection
content:

Repeat with goal S and with an isolated goal Z added as Z:[]. Keep the input graph, algorithm, neighbor order, expected route, observed route, action count and outcome in a short observation record. The ordinary route is S,A,G with two actions; start=goal has zero actions; Z is unreachable. Explain any mismatch using the first incorrect trace row. Record an unexecuted prediction as a prediction.

module: Unit 1: AI Landscape and State Representation
title: AI Landscape and State Representation Core Concepts
content:
## Represent states and transitions

A graph consists of states and connections between them. In a directed graph, S→A permits travel from S to A; it does not imply A→S. An adjacency dictionary represents the directed graph below. A state with no successors still appears with an empty list.

```python
graph = {"S": ["A", "B"], "A": ["G"], "B": [], "G": []}
```

## Worked route and state identity

The keys are stable state identifiers. The neighbor lists describe allowed transitions, in a reproducible order. S,A,G is a legal route; S,B,G is illegal because B has no edge to G. A route cost is the sum of its edge costs. In this unweighted example each transition costs one, so the route has cost two.

A Node object can hold an identifier and neighbors; a Graph object can look up nodes and add edges. Keep identifiers unique. Decide whether adding an edge creates a directed connection or two undirected connections, and implement that contract consistently. Check that both endpoint nodes exist before changing adjacency.

State equality is a modeling choice. For a locked-door problem, (room,has_key) distinguishes visits that allow different actions. A representation that keeps only room can discard a necessary return visit after obtaining a key.

A graph records possible transitions. The search frontier records which discovered states still need examination. Keeping those responsibilities separate allows BFS, DFS and cost-based searches to use the same problem model.

module: Unit 2: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition
title: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition Core Concepts
content:
## A frontier has an order

A stack removes its newest entry first: last in, first out. A queue removes its oldest entry first: first in, first out. Both can hold pending states, but they choose different next steps.

For a stack, `append` pushes and `pop()` removes the last list entry. For a queue, `collections.deque` supplies `append` and `popleft` without repeatedly shifting a list. An empty removal requires an explicit contract, such as a check before removal or a documented exception.

## Worked frontier trace

Start with S. Remove it and insert A then B. The stack next removes B; the queue next removes A. After a queue removes A and inserts C, its contents are [B,C], so B is next. This is the mechanism behind breadth-first exploration.

For DFS that should visit A before B, place B on the stack before A. State both the neighbor order and push order: saying only 'use a stack' does not determine the trace. A frontier entry can carry a state or an entire candidate route. The route representation makes a first experiment easier to inspect; a parent map avoids copying whole routes later.

The frontier may contain discovered states not yet expanded. A visited or discovered set prevents cycles from creating endless work. In BFS, marking on insertion ensures a state is queued once. A failed empty removal is a data-structure issue; finding no route after exhausting a valid frontier is a search outcome.

content:

title: Informed and Bounded Search Core Concepts
content:
## Limits, path costs and estimates

Depth counts edges from the start. Depth-limited search (DLS) explores at most a chosen depth. A goal exactly at the limit is accepted. A cutoff means a legal continuation was excluded by the limit; failure means all allowed cycle-free possibilities were exhausted. A cutoff alone does not prove a goal unreachable.

## Worked depth and cost cases

On S:[A,B], A:[C], C:[G], B:[], G:[], limits 0,1,2 produce cutoffs; limit 3 finds S,A,C,G. Iterative deepening repeats DLS at 0,1,2,3. It trades repeated shallow work for a small depth-first frontier. Track repeated states on the current path: a global closed set can incorrectly suppress a later shallower arrival.

For weighted paths, g(n) is accumulated route cost. Uniform-cost search orders by g. Greedy search orders by remaining-cost estimate h(n). A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n).

Use edges S-A=1, A-G=20, S-B=5, B-G=1 and estimates h(S)=0,h(A)=0,h(B)=1,h(G)=0. Greedy chooses S,A,G with cost 21. A* compares its cost 21 goal candidate with B's f=6, then finds S,B,G with cost 6. Low h alone does not account for an expensive incoming route.

For these finite examples use nonnegative finite costs. UCS stops when the cheapest queued goal is removed, rather than when any goal is first generated. A* additionally needs admissible estimates, h(goal)=0 and reopening after cheaper arrivals for its cheapest-path guarantee. An admissible estimate never exceeds the true cheapest remaining cost. Queue entries can become stale when a cheaper arrival is found; skip them.

title: Heuristics and Game AI Core Concepts
content:
## Evaluate a game tree

A game state includes the board and whose turn it is. Legal actions produce successor states. A terminal test stops expansion after a win or draw. Game-tree branches represent possible continuations, not promises about an opponent's actual move.

## Worked game positions

For Tic-Tac-Toe, number cells 0..8 in row-major order. X moves first. After two moves by each player, the board XX-/OO-/--- has X to move. Index2 wins immediately. On OO-/X--/-X-, X must block the top row at index 2 before considering a longer plan.

Choose a fixed scoring perspective. In the later O-agent studio, an O win scores +1, an X win -1 and a draw 0. At O turns maximize successor values; at X turns minimize them. The value of the empty board under complete optimal play is 0. Immediate win/block rules are a useful improvement over random choice, but fork positions show why they are not a complete strategy.

A heuristic estimates a nonterminal position when full expansion is too expensive. A minimax value from complete search is an exact outcome under the modeled rules and optimal future play. Neither is a probability of beating every human.

Create fresh child boards rather than mutating one board shared by siblings. Stop generating moves from terminal states, reject occupied cells and verify turn counts. Log each legal candidate and its score. A deterministic tie rule, such as lowest index, makes repeated comparisons reproducible.

title: Core Project: Heuristics and Game AI
content:
Use the linked tree-node example to inspect board state, turn, successors and terminal detection. Keep an untouched copy. Add an observation driver that prints legal move indices and child boards for XX-/OO-/--- and OO-/X--/-X-, both with X to move.

Confirm index 2 wins the first case and prevents O's immediate win in the second. A won or full board must offer no next moves. Changing one child must leave the original board and other children unchanged.

Add a lowest-index legal policy as a reproducible baseline. Record its selected move, then compare an immediate-win/block policy on the same two cases. Explain why two successful cases do not establish unbeatable play. Continue to the Tic-Tac-Toe studio for complete minimax, fork handling and its explicit O-centered scoring contract.

module: Unit 7: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI
title: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI Core Concepts
content:
## Features and evaluation

A feature is a measurable property of state: distance remaining, legal-move count or accumulated cost. A feature can help order choices, but it need not determine the goal. The blank can be in its goal cell while other puzzle tiles are wrong.

Evaluate against a stated contract. For search, record whether a valid route was returned, its edge cost, number of expanded states and whether the algorithm terminated. Separate invalid input from a valid unreachable problem. Compare algorithms on the same graphs, costs, neighbor order and stopping rule.

## Worked comparison

Use three solvable cases: the reference weighted graph has greedy cost 21 and A* cost 6; a single edge S-G=2 has cost 2 for both; start=goal has cost 0. Both solve 3/3, while mean route cost over those cases is 23/3 for greedy and 8/3 for A*. The success count hides the cost difference. Add a fourth valid case with an isolated G: both should report no route. Do not record that expected outcome as a discovered route.

A benchmark is a chosen collection of cases. Report per-case results and failure slices before a combined average. A set containing only direct edges cannot expose greedy's weighted detour. Timing also depends on machine and setup, so keep expansion counts and measurement conditions alongside elapsed time.

Responsible evaluation names affected people, a plausible failure and a response. A toy route planner that ignores stair access can return a mathematically short route that a traveler cannot use. Include accessibility in legal actions and allow a person to inspect or reject the proposed route. These toy fixtures establish behavior under their stated rules.

module: Unit 7: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI
title: Labels, Benchmarks, and Success Criteria
content:
## Decide what counts as success

A reachable label answers whether a legal route exists; it does not identify the cheapest route. Check reachability independently on a tiny graph before evaluating a policy. A candidate route passes validity only when its endpoints match the request and every consecutive transition is legal.

For a minimum-cost task, compare the reported cost with the sum of actual edge costs and with a trusted small-case optimum. A program that returns a valid cost 21 route when a cost 6 route exists passes reachability and fails minimum-cost success. A fast timeout passes neither requirement.

Keep the number of cases visible in each measure. Solved/solvable is a different fraction from correctly handled/all cases. An intentionally unreachable graph belongs in the latter measure; excluding every failure from an average can make a weak policy look better. Report failures and exclusions beside the average.

title: Capstone and Portfolio Build Core Concepts
content:
## A capstone with a checkable baseline

The required starting scope is a 3×3 sliding 8-puzzle. Its board contains tiles 1..8 and one blank, each exactly once. A legal move swaps the blank with one orthogonal neighbor. The goal is `123/456/78_`, where _ denotes the blank. Every move costs one.

## Worked two-move puzzle

Use start `123/456/_78`. Moving tile 7 left gives `123/456/7_8`; moving 8 left reaches the goal. This is a two-move route. Count transitions, rather than displayed boards: three boards represent two moves.

BFS provides a minimum-move baseline. A* can use Manhattan distance: for each numbered tile, add its row and column displacement from its goal cell; exclude the blank. The example start has estimate 2. One move changes the distance of one numbered tile by one, so this estimate never exceeds the minimum remaining moves. A* must still track cheapest arrivals and skip stale queued entries.

A valid board can be unsolvable. On an odd-width 3×3 board, remove the blank and count inverted numbered-tile pairs. Odd parity cannot reach the ordered goal. The board `123/456/87_` has one inversion and must return an unsolvable result.

A finishable capstone preserves the working baseline, adds one justified comparison and supplies a reproducible report. Changing presentation alone does not establish an algorithmic improvement. Route legality, move count and unsolvable detection remain acceptance conditions when a visualizer is added.

title: Core Project: Capstone and Portfolio Build
content:
Run the linked completed 8-puzzle reference with python3 main.py and reproduce its two-move default. Create a separate capstone working copy and preserve the reference.

Record BFS and A* results for `123/456/_78`, the goal `123/456/78_`, and unsolvable `123/456/87_`. Expect two moves, zero moves and an explicit unsolvable outcome. Validate that each returned board uses every tile exactly once and each transition is one orthogonal blank swap.

Add one chosen valid board with at least four legal moves from the goal, recording how it was generated. Compare expanded states and returned move counts for BFS and Manhattan A* under the same limits. A scramble can immediately undo a move, so scramble length alone is not a shortest-distance label.

Deliver the board fixtures, reproducible commands, route validator, result table and a short explanation of the chosen improvement and limitations. If time or expansion limits stop a run, record an incomplete result rather than an invented route. Maze or marble-game alternatives retain the same baseline/comparison/report requirements with their own rules.

title: Build for Explanation, Not Just Output
content:
## Make the result inspectable

A puzzle report connects an initial board to a sequence of legal moves. Keep the initial board, each move, resulting board, goal check and total move count. A trace also records why the frontier selected the next state: queue order for BFS, or g,h and g+h for A*.

Use a result table with the same fields for both algorithms: case, outcome, valid route, moves, expanded states and limit. Keep the original raw output with the report. A summary that says 'A* is faster' needs matching inputs and measurements; a smaller expansion count on one board supports a claim about that board.

If the next project studies learned models, distinguish explicit search rules from fitted behavior. If it studies data analysis, distinguish the recorded algorithm observations from the questions asked of that data. The capstone's explanation should identify a justified next investigation from the observed results.

title: The Marble Game AI: Core Concepts

Verify piles 1,4,5,7: take 1 at 1, no guaranteed win at 4, take 1 at 5 and take 3 at 7. Compare the exact policy with lowest-legal or seeded-random choice. content: Derive why pile 4 loses and pile 5 wins from the smaller positions. Explain why the positive multiples of 4 remain losing under these rules. Check that each candidate score describes the resulting opponent state. State how a last-take-loses variation would require a different terminal rule and new evaluation.

title: AI Level 1 Reference Guide
content:
## Search assumptions

A problem identifies state, legal actions, initial state, goal and cost. A frontier selects pending work; a discovered set and parent map record progress. On finite graphs, record cycle handling and tie rules alongside a trace.

BFS minimizes edge count when steps have equal cost. DFS is a reachability method and can return a longer route. UCS minimizes nonnegative finite route cost. A* orders by g+h; its cheapest-path contract requires an admissible estimate, h(goal)=0 and correct handling of cheaper arrivals. Greedy orders by h and does not generally minimize route cost.

Depth limits count edges. A goal at the limit is valid. A cutoff records an excluded continuation; it differs from exhausted failure.

References: [UC Berkeley uninformed search](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/search/uninformed.html) and [informed search](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/search/informed.html).

title: AI Level 1 Core Skills
content:
## Debug a state transition

Check representation before frontier policy. A missing key, incorrect turn or shared mutable board changes the problem even when the search loop is correct.

For a returned route, verify the initial state, goal and every legal edge. Recompute cost from the edges. For each parent link, confirm that the parent could generate the child. A visited-order list cannot replace these checks.

Compare the first differing trace row with a hand calculation. Inspect its selected state, pending frontier, cost and new discoveries. Copy mutable trace collections to preserve earlier snapshots. Change one condition at a time: neighbor order, edge cost, limit or heuristic.

For game search, state the player perspective and terminal utility. The maximizing and minimizing turns alternate under that fixed perspective. [UC Berkeley minimax](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook/games/minimax.html) develops this rule.

title: AI Level 1 Next Topics
content:
## Extend a completed investigation

Keep a baseline case and its raw result before changing the problem. Transfer practice changes a state space or constraint; an extension adds a comparison or diagnostic. The eighteen optional project packs supply their own readings, fixtures and role files.

Choose a graph extension for reachability or cost, a puzzle extension for representation and heuristics, or a game extension for evaluation. Record the new input, prediction, actual result and reason for any difference. Preserve the original completion checks.

The optional reference bank contains completed demonstrations and earlier variants. Copy a completed example for an experiment, then implement and verify the assigned modification.

title: AI Level 1 Boundaries
content:
## Bound the claim

An algorithm's guarantee depends on its model and assumptions. A shortest walking route can be unsuitable when legal actions ignore stairs or closed doors. Identify those constraints before using a result to guide a decision.

Use fictional graphs, puzzles and game positions in these labs. A claim about learning from data requires an actual training process; these search and rule examples use authored transitions and scores.

A benchmark reports its cases, success contract, failures and limits. Keep timing conditions, random seeds and tie rules reproducible. A timed-out run remains incomplete. Human review can reject a result when important constraints are missing.

title: AI Level 1 Prerequisite Check
content:
## Python prerequisite check

The course uses functions, lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples and simple classes. A dictionary retrieves a state's neighbors; a set tracks discovery; a tuple can act as a stable board key. Lists and dictionaries are mutable, so copy snapshots that must retain an earlier state.

For a stack, use append then pop. For a queue, use collections.deque with append and popleft. A single item is removed first by either structure. Inserting A then B exposes the ordering difference.

Trace insert S, remove, insert A, insert B, remove, insert C, remove, remove. The stack returns S,B,C,A; the queue returns S,A,B,C. Check for empty before another removal or use a documented exception.

[Python deque documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.deque) describes these operations.

title: AI Level 1 Pathway Map
content:
## Choose a continuation

AI Level 1 develops explicit state, rules, search, heuristics and game evaluation. Machine Learning develops fitted models and their validation. Data Science in Python develops data questions, preparation, analysis and interpretation.

An algorithmic continuation can deepen search and proofs. A learned-model continuation can use meaningful state features as inputs with training and evaluation data. A data-focused continuation can analyze recorded experiments while retaining denominators and failure cases.

Keep a portfolio example with reproducible inputs, a working baseline, one justified improvement and an explanation of limits. That evidence identifies what is ready to build on and what needs further practice.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants Core Concepts
content:
## Compare implementations

The reference bank provides optional graph, class, frontier and game demonstrations. The canonical Tic-Tac-Toe tree and its copy are different variants. The two marble-tree copies retain the same implementation; their filenames do not establish different learning outcomes.

The core studios evaluate reached Tic-Tac-Toe states with caching and marble positions from zero upward. Earlier tree examples eagerly construct future states. Compare initialization cost, repeated states, candidate scores and selected moves on the same legal positions. Keep each version's scoring perspective and terminal rule explicit.

Small stack, queue and class examples refresh prerequisites. The visualization examples use networkx and matplotlib in the local environment from the setup reading. To investigate an algorithm without graphics, use the supplied adjacency lists and search traces.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants

title: Reference Archive: AI Level 1 Workspace
content:
Choose one named example from the repository archive: FAI-Stacks, FAI-Queues or FAI6-Magic-Portals. Open that folder's main.py and record whether it is a completed example or an unfinished exercise. Compare the run with the prediction: the stack removes 4,3,2,1; the queue removes 1,2,3,4; Tokyo to London needs three portals. Explain the first operation that determines the result. title: Object Refresh: Dog Class
content:
Use the linked completed Dog example to practice independent object state. Create Dog("Fido",4) and Dog("Luna",2). Print each dog's name, age, tricks and sitting state. Call learn_trick("roll") only on Fido, then call sit_down() and stand_up() while printing get_state() after each change.

Checkpoints: Fido's tricks become ["roll"], Luna's stay [], and the two states read "Fido is sitting" then "Fido is standing". With no learned tricks, do_trick() returns the named dog's no-tricks message. With exactly one trick it returns that trick without a random-choice ambiguity. Add a second trick and verify that every returned choice belongs to that dog's list. Keep the before/after observations and explain why tricks must be an instance attribute.

title: Object Refresh: Deck of Cards
content:
Use the completed Card and Deck example. Before shuffling, collect the pairs (card.value,card.suit) from deck.deck. Check that there are 52 distinct pairs: values 1 through 13 in each of Spades, Hearts, Clubs and Diamonds. Shuffle, then compare the pair collection with the original; the order can change while membership stays the same.

Draw one card with draw_card() and check that 51 remain. Draw the rest, confirming that each original card appears exactly once. A further draw prints the empty-deck message and returns None. Repeat with a fresh deck so the previous experiment's mutations cannot affect the next one. Save the checks and explain why observing one shuffled order cannot establish whether all orders are equally likely.

module: Unit 1: AI Landscape and State Representation
title: Project: Node and Graph Class
content:
Complete Graph in the linked starter using its supplied Node class. Store nodes in the graph dictionary, add nodes through add_node(), and implement add_edge() as an undirected connection between two registered nodes. Implement __str__() so the nodes and their neighbor keys can be inspected.

Create nodes a,b,c,d, register all four and add edges a-b and b-c. Checkpoints: a lists b; b lists a and c; c lists b; d has no neighbors. An edge to an unregistered node must produce a clear failure without changing existing adjacency. State whether repeated edges are allowed and demonstrate that contract. Keep this object exercise separate from Unit 1's directed adjacency dictionary: one undirected edge must be traversable in both directions. Submit the completed starter and these observations.

module: Unit 1: AI Landscape and State Representation
title: Project: Graphs with Network Visualization
content:
Run the linked completed example in the local graphics environment from the setup reading. It produces basic_graph.png and acyclic_graph.png. For the first graph, list vertices a,b,c,d and undirected edges a-b,a-c,c-d,d-a. For the second, list a-b,a-c,d-a. Compare the saved images with those exact lists; drawing positions can vary between runs.

Checkpoints: both images contain four labeled vertices. The first has the cycle a,c,d,a; the second is connected with three edges and has no cycle. Remove edge d-a from the first graph in a separate copy and predict how its cycle changes before generating another image. Keep the two originals and changed output with their edge lists. The image shows adjacency; it does not record a search algorithm's visit order.

module: Unit 1: AI Landscape and State Representation
title: Project: Airports Problem
content:
Run the linked directed weighted airport example. Starting in Boston, enter ny, sf, la. The travel times are 1,6,1 hours, so the printed total must be eight hours. Run again with dc, s, sf, la; times 2,7,3,1 total thirteen hours. Record the selected keys and accumulated time after each flight.

Checkpoints: the eight-hour route and thirteen-hour route both arrive in Los Angeles. An unavailable destination must repeat the choice without moving or charging time. Spaces and letter case are normalized by the input handler. Explain why a flight from one city does not imply a reverse flight in this graph. Add a new airport and one outgoing flight in a copy; document its time and test the new transition.

module: Unit 2: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition
title: Project: Practice with Stacks
content:
Use the linked completed stack exercises as examples, then write independent checks for their behavior. Push integers 1 through 10 and repeatedly pop; the removal order is 10 down to 1. Trace the contents after every removal. Check isPalindrome("racecar"), isPalindrome("mom") and isPalindrome("hello world"); expect True, True and False. State that the supplied comparison is literal and case-sensitive.

For evaluateExpression(), check "2 3 +" gives 5, "1 3 -" gives -2 and "3 5 + 4 *" gives 32. Explain why subtraction uses the second popped operand first. In a separate version, reject expressions with too few operands or multiple leftover values. Keep valid results and the chosen invalid-input behavior in the observation record.

module: Unit 2: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition
title: Project: Practice with Queues
content:
Trace the linked completed queue exercises before changing them. Enqueue 1 through 10 and remove from the front; expect 1 through 10 in the same order. In buildQueueString(), each ordinary character enters the queue and each * removes its front character into the output. Check "H*ELL**O**" produces "HELLO"; also trace "AB**" to "AB".

For getEvens([1,2,6,5,4,6]), expect [2,6,4,6], preserving order and duplicates. The supplied function consumes its input list; show that the original list is empty afterward. In a separate variant, preserve the caller's list while producing the same result. Test an empty list and an all-odd list. Record how an unmatched * is handled before adding validation for that case.

module: Unit 2: Stacks, Queues, and Traversal Intuition
title: Project: Stacks and Queues Reference
content:
Trace the four-value queue in the linked reference. It appends 1,2,3,4, peeks at index zero, removes the front value, checks emptiness and then drains the queue. Write down each printed value before execution. The sequence is 1,1,False,2,3,4: peeking observes the first 1 without removing it.

Make an independent stack version with the same inserted values, using the last position for both peek and pop. Its corresponding sequence is 4,4,False,3,2,1. Check the length after peeking and after removal to distinguish observation from mutation. Guard peek and removal on an empty container with a stated exception or return value. Save the two small versions and their traces as a reference for frontier ordering.

title: Project: Implement DFS
content:
Run both DFS methods in the linked example on its undirected graph with edges a-b,a-c,b-d,b-e. The iterative version appends neighbors in their stored order and pops from the end; expect a,c,b,e,d. The recursive version follows the first unvisited neighbor immediately; expect a,b,d,e,c. Record when each node becomes visited.

Checkpoints: both methods visit the same five vertices once despite their different orders. Add an isolated vertex z and verify that traversal from a does not reach it. Add an edge e-a to make a cycle and confirm termination. In a separate copy, reverse the iterative neighbor insertion order and compare the new trace. Explain why a valid DFS traversal need not be a shortest route to every vertex.

title: Project: Implement BFS
content:
Use the linked BFS example on the undirected graph a-b,a-c,b-d,b-e. Predict its queue after expanding a and after expanding b. The resulting visit order is a,b,c,d,e because newly discovered neighbors join the back. Record each first discovery and its parent.

Extend a copy to return a route to a named target rather than only printing all reachable nodes. The route a,b,e contains two edges. Check start=a,goal=a returns [a], and an added isolated target z has no route. Mark a node discovered when enqueueing it so a cycle does not create repeated queued copies. Retain the original traversal example and the route-returning variant with these checks. State the equal-edge-cost condition behind BFS's minimum-edge guarantee.

title: Project: Magic Portals
content:
Run the linked city graph and verify its four distances: San Francisco to Dubai is 1, Tokyo to Dubai is 2, New York to Dubai is 2 and Tokyo to London is 3. Each graph edge counts as one action regardless of geographical distance. Draw the city adjacency that supports the Tokyo,San Francisco,Washington D.C,London route.

Checkpoints: a city to itself takes zero portals; an added isolated city is unreachable; a city not registered in the graph is rejected. The supplied method returns None when no route is found. In a copy, also return the sequence of city keys and verify every consecutive pair is connected. Keep the distance result separate from the route itself. Explain why the shared visited set prevents cycles from being explored forever.

title: Project: Maze Solver
content:
The linked folder is a starter: main.py draws the maze, while maze.py prints a supplied path; neither file implements search. Retain both files in the same project. Add a solver in a separate helper or main.py using cell coordinates (row,column), start (0,0), goal (2,0) and moves through open passages only.

For a hand-checkable independent representation, use adjacency (0,0):[(0,1),(1,0)], (0,1):[(0,0),(0,2)], (0,2):[(0,1),(1,2)], (1,0):[(0,0),(1,1)], (1,1):[(1,0),(2,1)], (1,2):[(0,2),(2,2)], (2,0):[(2,1)], (2,1):[(1,1),(2,0),(2,2)], (2,2):[(1,2),(2,1)]. BFS reaches the goal in four moves via (1,1). Record parents and render the recovered path. Treat quicksand costs as a later weighted extension; first verify legal movement and unreachable/start-equals-goal cases.

title: Project: Implement DLS
content:
Trace the linked depth-limited search on edges a-b,a-c,b-e,c-d,d-e. Run limits 0,1,2,3. The printed orders are respectively a; a,c,b; a,c,d,b,e; and a,c,d,e,b. Depth counts edges from the start. Record the pending (node,depth) pairs to explain each limit's reachable set.

The method records the best depth discovered for each node. Explain why reaching a node later by a shallower route can permit further expansion even if that node was already printed. Check a negative limit produces no visits, a zero limit includes only the start, and limit 4 reaches the same set as limit 3. Retain the observations and add a target-returning variant that distinguishes a found route from a depth cutoff.

title: Project: Implement IDS
content:
Run the linked iterative-deepening example with max_depth=4. It performs depth-limited traversals for limits 0 through 4, including both endpoints. On its supplied graph the lines are a; a,c,b; a,c,d,b,e; a,c,d,e,b; and a,c,d,e,b. Record each limit and its printed order in a table.

Compare this repeated work with one depth-limited traversal at limit 4. Explain why earlier depths are visited again and why visited/depth information must reset between iterations. Add a target-returning variant that stops at the first depth where the target is found; for target e in the supplied graph that depth is 2. Check start=goal at depth zero and an isolated target with a finite maximum depth. Report cutoff separately from a proof that no route exists.

title: Project: Implement UCS
content:
Trace the linked uniform-cost search on weighted edges a-b:3,a-c:5,a-e:15,b-d:1,b-e:6. Edges are undirected in this implementation. The settled nodes and costs are a:0,b:3,d:4,c:5,e:9; the cheaper route to e is a,b,e rather than the direct edge of cost 15.

Record each removed priority and explain why a later queued copy of e is skipped after e has been settled. Add a separate isolated node and verify that it is absent from traversal started at a. Add a zero-cost edge in a copy and compare the resulting costs with hand sums. Preserve the nonnegative-cost assumption; negative edges require a different method. Submit the trace and a route-reconstruction extension with an explicit no-route result.

title: Project: Compare A* and Greedy Search
content:
Run the linked A* example and the Greedy Search Lab example using their shared undirected graph S-A:1,A-G:20,S-B:5,B-G:1. Their heuristic values are S:0,A:0,B:1,G:0. A* orders pending states by g+h; greedy uses h alone. Predict each next expansion from its priority.

Checkpoints: A* returns S,B,G at cost 6; greedy returns S,A,G at cost 21. Compare routes using the same edge-cost sum, and record expansion orders separately from returned paths. Repeat with a start-equals-goal request and an isolated target added to each graph. Change all heuristics to zero in a copy and explain the change in A* ordering. A favorable result on this graph alone does not establish heuristic quality on other problems.

title: Project: Greedy Search Lab
content:
Use the linked completed greedy example with graph S-A:1,A-G:20,S-B:5,B-G:1 and estimates S:0,A:0,B:1,G:0. Trace discovery of A and B after expanding S. The smaller estimate at A is selected first; G is then selected, yielding S,A,G at cost 21.

Checkpoints: independently sum the returned path's edge costs. Compare it with S,B,G at cost 6 to demonstrate the cost of that choice. Verify start=goal returns a zero-cost single-node path and an isolated goal returns no path with cost None. In a copy, change A's estimate to 2 and predict which route greedy finds before running. Record the actual route and expansions. Explain that selecting by an estimate alone gives no general minimum-cost guarantee.

module: Unit 5: Rule-Based Systems and Puzzle Framing
title: Project: Adventure Game State Tracker
content:
Run the linked completed directed adventure. Check the paths start→leave and start→explore→check it out; they reach different terminal messages. Enter an unavailable choice first, then a valid choice. The handler must repeat the prompt without changing the current node, and it accepts surrounding spaces and letter-case changes.

Extend a copy with an inventory-bearing state (location,has_key). Add hall→store, store→hall while acquiring a key, and hall→outside only when the key is present. Check hall→outside is blocked before collection; hall→store→hall→outside succeeds afterward. Keep the two hall states distinct when searching: location alone cannot capture the gate. Submit the state transitions and recorded paths. This inventory rule is the new extension; the supplied theme-park example represents location choices.

module: Unit 5: Rule-Based Systems and Puzzle Framing
title: Project: Puzzle Solver Warmup
content:
Use the linked completed sliding-puzzle example to inspect representation before building a larger solver. Its board contains strings "1" through "8" and a single space for the blank. Set the start rows to ["1","2","3"],["4","5","6"],[" ","7","8"]. The goal rows end with ["7","8"," "].

Checkpoints: generate_neighbors() produces only boards formed by one orthogonal blank swap, without changing the original board. Moving the blank right twice solves the supplied case in two moves. The numbered-tile Manhattan estimate is 2 initially and 0 at the goal. Swap 7 and 8 in the goal to obtain an unsolvable odd-parity board. Record what bfs() and astarsearch() return for each case, including their different no-solution result formats, and explain how repeated states are recognized.

module: Unit 5: Rule-Based Systems and Puzzle Framing
title: Project: Book Rule System
content:
The linked example implements friendship groups with FriendGraph; its task is connected-component counting. Use the two supplied graphs and predict count_groups(): the first returns 1 and the second returns 3. In the second graph, a,b,c form one component while d and e each form their own.

Build another graph with vertices p,q,r,s and only edge p-q. It has three components; adding r-s leaves two, and adding q-r leaves one. Check an empty graph has zero groups and a graph with one isolated vertex has one. Record the visited set after each component search. Explain why a friendship edge is undirected in this example. Submit the component memberships with their counts; the supplied source counts connectivity rather than inferring book recommendations.

title: Project: Tic-Tac-Toe Tree Nodes
content:
Inspect the linked TreeNode example. A node stores a 3×3 board, the player whose turn comes next and a children list; empty cells use "-". Its supplied empty board returns (None,False) from check_win(), while the diagonal X board returns ("X",True). Draw the diagonal that establishes the win.

Add independent row, column and draw cases. For a draw, use rows X,O,X / X,O,O / O,X,X and expect ("draw",True). Create one legal child of the empty root by placing X in the center, switching the child's player to O and preserving the root board. Check that modifying a copied child cannot change its parent. Keep terminal-result checks separate from move selection: this file supplies a node representation, not a complete opponent.

title: Project: Random Tic-Tac-Toe AI
content:
Use the linked completed random-opponent program as a baseline. Empty cells use "-", X moves first and the computer plays O. Record one complete legal game, including the position before each random move and the set of empty cells available then. Each chosen move must occupy exactly one previously empty cell.

To inspect tree generation without building the entire empty-board tree, use a near-terminal root with rows X,X,- / O,O,- / -,-,- and X to move. Its legal first children place X in one of five empty cells; placing X at (0,2) ends the game immediately. Compare those children with the parent to check copying and turn switching. Repeat recorded trials with a fixed random seed when comparing implementations; a seed supports reproducibility, not a claim of optimal play.

title: Project: Unbeatable Tic-Tac-Toe AI
content:
Use the linked minimax example with "-" for empty cells. Scores are from O's perspective: O wins +10, X wins -10 and a draw is 0. O maximizes and X minimizes. Start with near-terminal positions so the full continuation tree is small enough to inspect.

For rows X,X,- / O,O,- / -,-,- with X to move, the best child places X at (0,2) for an immediate win. For rows O,O,- / X,-,- / -,X,- with X to move, the best child blocks (0,2). Check a terminal root has no best child and retains its terminal score. Then compare play from the empty board with an independently optimal opponent; optimal play draws. Save the boards, chosen children and score perspective alongside the source.

title: Project: Marble Game AI
content:
Use the linked five-marble game. A turn removes 1,2 or 3 marbles without taking more than remain; taking the last marble wins. TreeNode(num_marbles,is_AI) records whose turn is next. Its score is positive for a human win and negative for an AI win, so AI turns minimize the score.

Checkpoints: one remaining marble is winning for the player to move; four remaining marbles are losing against optimal opposition. From five, the winning first move removes one and leaves four. Inspect legal children and best_child for these small positions before playing the interactive version. Check no child has a negative count and a zero-marble node is terminal. Record a complete five-marble game and explain the terminal score using the next-player flag.

module: Unit 7: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI
title: Project: Search Strategy Comparison Lab
content:
Compare the linked greedy example with A* from the informed-search unit. Use three shared cases: the weighted S,A,B,G graph with costs 1,20,5,1; a chain S→M→G with unit costs and zero estimates; and start=goal. Expected route costs are greedy [21,2,0] and A* [6,2,0].

Record returned route, summed cost, expanded-state count and largest frontier for each run. Add measurement counters in separate copies and state whether the goal removal is counted. If timing is reported, use the same interpreter and repeated runs; separate construction from search. The mean costs are 23/3 and 8/3 for these cases. Report unreachable cases separately rather than averaging None as zero. Explain one limitation of comparing algorithms on only these three fixtures.

module: Unit 7: Features, Evaluation, and Responsible AI
title: Project: Water Jug Riddle
content:
Run the linked 3-litre/5-litre jug example. A state (x,y) records water in the 3L and 5L jugs, with 0≤x≤3 and 0≤y≤5. Legal actions fill, empty or pour from one jug into the other until the source empties or destination fills. The goal is four litres in the 5L jug.

Checkpoints: verify the six-action route (0,0)→(0,5)→(3,2)→(0,2)→(2,0)→(2,5)→(3,4). Each transition must match one legal action. Compare greedy_solve() and a_star_solve() by route length and states searched. The remaining-volume estimate used by greedy can overestimate actions; A* uses its separate admissible estimate. Check an already solved state (0,4) returns a zero-action route, and explain why both jug amounts belong in the visited-state key.

title: Capstone: 8-Puzzle Solver
content:
Run the linked complete solver, then build a documented variant with the same public inputs. Boards are 3×3 lists of strings "1" through "8" plus one space. Use start rows ["1","2","3"],["4","5","6"],[" ","7","8"] and the goal ending ["7","8"," "]. Both bfs_solve() and a_star_solve() should return a two-move path.

Checkpoints: every adjacent returned board differs by one legal blank swap; the first and last boards match the requested endpoints. Check an already solved board returns zero moves. Swapping 7 and 8 at the goal must be rejected as unsolvable before a large search. Compare states searched using the same counting convention and confirm Manhattan distance excludes the blank. Deliver the source, three case results and an explanation of the parity and heuristic assumptions.

title: Capstone Option: Maze Solver Showcase
content:
Extend the earlier maze starter after completing its legal-move BFS solver. Keep the provided main.py and maze.py together. Use the same start (0,0), goal (2,0) and passage graph from the Maze Solver assignment; the unweighted shortest route uses four moves and crosses quicksand at (1,1).

Define weighted cost explicitly: leaving (1,1) costs 5 and leaving any other cell costs 1. The four-move route costs 8, while the six-move route along the top and right side costs 6. Compare BFS with uniform-cost search using these exact weights. Check the returned path against walls before displaying it, and report both move count and total cost. Add start=goal and unreachable-target cases. Deliver the visual trace with the passage dictionary and measurement results.

title: Capstone Option: Marble Game Strategy Lab
content:
Extend the linked complete marble opponent by comparing a random legal policy with full minimax on starting piles 1 through 8. Each move removes 1,2 or 3; taking the last marble wins. Record the player to move as part of every state. Against optimal play, positive multiples of four are losing starting positions; every other listed count has a move leaving a multiple of four.

Checkpoints: 1,2,3 each have an immediate winning move; 4 is losing; from 5 remove one. Verify legal children and terminal handling before collecting game results. Use a fixed seed for repeated random-policy trials and alternate which policy moves first. Record wins by starting pile and starting player. Explain why a random opponent's win rate does not establish strength against optimal opposition.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: Special Graphs
content:
Run the linked completed graphics example in the setup reading's local environment. Retain basic_graph.png, acyclic_graph.png, weighted_graph.png and directed_graph.png. Compare each image with the edge list immediately above its drawing code; layout coordinates may change between runs.

Checkpoints: the weighted graph uses a-b:3,a-c:0,c-d:1,d-a:6, so a→c→d costs 1 while a→d costs 6. The directed graph has a→b,a→c,c→d,d→a; b cannot reach a because it has no outgoing edge. Verify those claims with adjacency or a manual route before adding programmatic checks. A zero-weight edge remains an edge. Submit the four images, route sums and one changed graph whose reachability or minimum-cost route differs from the original.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: Practice with Stacks (Reference Bank)
content:
Use this small stack reference to isolate push, peek and pop from the larger expression exercises. It appends 1,2,3,4, peeks at the last value, removes it, checks emptiness and drains the remaining stack. Predict the print sequence 4,4,False,3,2,1 before running.

Checkpoints: peek leaves length four; the first pop leaves length three; the final stack is empty. Add a safe-pop wrapper with a stated empty-stack result and test it once more after draining. Compare the same operations with the queue reference from Unit 2 to identify exactly which endpoint changes. Keep the traces beside both versions. As a small extension, insert a new value after two removals and predict the remaining order before execution.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: BankAccount Class
content:
Use the linked completed BankAccount object as a state-transition exercise. Create an account with interest_rate=0.10, deposit 1000, calculate_interest(), withdraw 1000 and attempt to withdraw 150. Expected balances are 1000,1100,100,100; the last withdrawal reports insufficient funds and preserves the balance.

Checkpoints: a separate account starts at zero and is unaffected by the first account's changes. Zero deposits and withdrawals leave the balance unchanged. Negative or nonfinite amounts raise ValueError before mutation. In a separate copy, document the order of operations for two consecutive interest calculations and compare their result with one calculation. Save the transition log and explain which attributes define account state. This is a class-behavior example; its simplified arithmetic does not specify a real bank's money or interest rules.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: DFS with a Stack Class
content:
Compare the linked Stack API with the earlier list-based DFS. The stack's push appends, peek observes the last value, pop removes it and isEmpty() reports whether values remain. In the supplied check, pushing 1,2,3 yields peek 3, followed by pops 3,2,1 and True for emptiness.

For graph edges a-b,a-c,b-d,b-e, dfs_with_stack_class(a) prints a,c,b,e,d. Trace the Stack calls and compare that order with the earlier iterative DFS under the same neighbor insertion order. Add edge e-a and verify each reachable vertex is still printed once. Test an empty graph and an isolated registered start separately. Submit the API trace and traversal comparison, explaining which changes concern data representation and which concern the search algorithm.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: BFS with a Queue Class
content:
Compare the linked Queue API with the earlier list-based BFS. enqueue appends, peek observes the front, dequeue removes the front and isEmpty() reports whether values remain. In the supplied check, enqueueing 1,2,3 yields peek 1, followed by removals 1,2,3 and True for emptiness.

For graph edges a-b,a-c,b-d,b-e, bfs_with_queue_class(a) prints a,b,c,d,e. Trace the Queue calls and compare them with the earlier BFS using the same adjacency order. Add a cycle and confirm discovery-time visited tracking prevents duplicate queued vertices. Test an empty graph and an isolated registered start separately. Extend a copy to return a route to e and verify its two edges. Submit the trace and explain why a different queue representation preserves FIFO behavior.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: Updated Tic-Tac-Toe AI
content:
Compare the linked shared-state game graph with the earlier full game tree. This variant uses a space for an empty cell, while the earlier version uses "-". It stores previously generated board nodes so different move orders can reuse the same position. Record that representation difference before copying a board between versions.

Checkpoints: use X,X,blank / O,O,blank / blank,blank,blank with X to move and verify the immediate winning move at (0,2). Also check the forced block from O,O,blank / X,blank,blank / blank,X,blank. Compare scores and legal moves with the earlier minimax after converting empty markers. The program can save its own data.pkl cache; compare first construction with loading only that locally generated cache. Report node reuse separately from search quality and record which work each timing includes.

module: Unit 9: Repo Extension Bank and Canonical Variants
title: Extension: Two-Player Marble Game
content:
Use the linked two-player five-marble example before adding an automated opponent. Each player may remove 1,2 or 3 without taking more than remain; whoever takes the last marble wins. Trace a game in which Player 1 takes one, Player 2 takes three and Player 1 takes one. The final winner is Player 1.

Checkpoints: no child state has a negative count; a zero-count state has no children. Try taking four or taking zero and verify the game repeats the current player's choice without changing the pile. Draw the full legal move tree from a pile of three, labeling whose turn follows every edge. Keep the transcript and tree. As an extension, choose moves that leave a multiple of four and explain the connection with the later minimax opponent.
